articles.title: A phase decoder for reconstructing missing muscle activity
articles.content: Upper-limb assistive devices are commonly controlled with electromyographic (EMG) signals, but nerve injury, muscle loss, or practical limits on electrode placement can leave only a few usable signals, which constrains the decoding of intended movements. Here, we introduce a decoder that reconstructs missing muscle activations from sparse EMGs using a two-stage real-time approach: (1) estimating ongoing movement phase from available signals, and (2) retrieving corresponding muscle activations from a library of pre-recorded muscle activity templates. In proof-of-concept tests, neurologically intact participants (N=4) performed object-transfer tasks under simulated denervation conditions. The decoder accurately estimated movement phase (median root-mean-square error [RMSE] <0.17 of movement duration) and reconstructed missing muscle activations (RMSE 0.08-0.34; correlation up to 0.97) within ~2 ms, in a previously unseen participant. The results indicate that template based reconstruction could leverage sparse EMG for low latency control of assistive technology.
articles.author: Bahdasariants, S., Yakovenko, S.

articles.title: State-dependent emergence of coupling between oscillatory and aperiodic neural activity
articles.content: Neural oscillations and aperiodic activity are two quintessential mesoscopic-level features arising from shared circuits, yet what governs their relationship remains unclear. Here we show that coupling between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent is sporadic and state-dependent. Bias-reduced analyses of 3,245 intracranial contacts from 61 awake subjects showed significant coupling in only <13% of contacts per band. A connectome-constrained dynamical model predicted that neither changes of input to local circuit nor removal of long-range connections modulated the coupling; whereas stronger local inhibitory feedback drove covariation between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent. The model predictions were supported by three independent experiments: transcranial stimulation shifted each component independently and focal ablation of remote cortical tissues did not change coupling; whereas coupling emerged during seizures that altered local excitatory-inhibitory balance. These results suggest that the relation between periodic and aperiodic neural activity is neither intrinsically independent nor coupled, but determined by local circuit states.
articles.author: Lu, Y., Li, Z., Mao, H., He, X., Liu, D., Chen, J., Tao, L., Xiao, Z.-C., Tian, X.

articles.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
articles.content: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.
articles.author: Szakacs, H., Gombos, F., Kringelbach, M. L., Deco, G., Kovacs, I.

articles.title: Paraquat Inhalation Produces Male-Biased Dopaminergic Neuron Loss and Motor Deficits in Mice: Relevance to Parkinsons Disease
articles.content: Long-term exposure to paraquat (PQ), a widely used herbicide, has been linked to increased risk of Parkinsons Disease (PD) in agricultural workers and rural communities in the United States (US), findings further supported by experimental animal studies. Although banned in many countries across the globe, PQ remains widely used in the US. Inhalation of PQ has been known to induce systemic organ failure at acute concentrations. However, prolonged low-dose inhalation from agricultural spraying and pesticide drift has not been readily evaluated for its potential to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases in vivo. Instead, many experimental studies have relied on systemic routes of exposure, which do not effectively replicate the most common route of exposure to PQ in the environment. In the current study, Parkinsonian features were examined in mice that had been exposed via whole-body inhalation to PQ aerosol for either 40 or 60 days. Levels of PQ in brain were highest in olfactory bulb, followed by frontal cortex and then brainstem in both sexes. After 60 days of exposure, male-specific impairments in locomotor activity were observed, in addition to reductions in striatal dopamine, in substantia nigra tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and number of TH+ dopaminergic neurons, the latter being considered the primary basis of PD, along with increased olfactory bulb -synuclein levels. As such, these studies confirm the dopaminergic neurotoxicity of inhaled PQ. These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.
articles.author: Reina-Gonzalez, P. J., Boos, J. R., Abu-Salah, A., Anchan, A., Strazdins, R., Ay, M., Shah, A., Chalupa, D., Richardson, J. J., Sarkar, S., Cory-Slechta, D.

articles.title: Imipramine binds to amyloid-β and extends the survival of Alzheimer's disease patients
articles.content: Background Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays numerous roles in the pathogenic pathway to Alzheimer's disease (AD). We previously performed a high-throughput screen and identified the antidepressant imipramine as an inhibitor of the interaction between apoE and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}). We also found that imipramine use to treat depression in AD patients was associated with better Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores. Here we studied the mechanisms by which imipramine inhibits the AD pathogenic pathway and investigated its effect on mortality in AD patients. Methods Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to characterize the interaction between imipramine and A{beta} monomers. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived AD cerebral organoids (COs) and transgenic AD rats treated with imipramine underwent neuropathological evaluation, while rat learning and memory were assessed in the Morris Water Maze. AD patient mortality in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Imipramine inhibits the apoE-A{beta} interaction by binding directly to A{beta} monomers. Imipramine reduces A{beta} accumulation and neuronal cell loss in AD COs. Imipramine-treated female AD rats had enhanced reference memory and increased hippocampal cellularity and cholinergic neurotransmission. AD patients prescribed imipramine had reduced all-cause mortality over 10 years relative to those prescribed other tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), non-TCA antidepressants, or no antidepressants. Conclusions The findings support the conclusions that: a) the mechanism by which apoE confers risk for AD is by catalyzing the polymerization of A{beta} into neurotoxic species, b) targeting apoE is a promising, underappreciated strategy for the prevention of AD, c) imipramine should be used more frequently to treat depression in AD clinical practice, and d) imipramine should be evaluated in prospective trials, particularly in APOE4 carriers, as a potential method to improve cognition and reduce mortality in AD.
articles.author: Johnson, N. R., Beham, J., Sillau, S., Read, J., Wang, A. C.-J., Ahmed, M. M., Quang, D., Stephenson, D., Henen, M., Vogeli, B., Chial, H. J., Welty, R., Vugmeyster, L., Potter, H.

articles.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
articles.content: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.
articles.author: Fallah, K., Chen, H. N., Singha, R., Kong, E., Turi, G. F., Losonczy, A., Zabeh, E.

articles.title: Hmox1/CO regulates retina regeneration via modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling and induction of vaspb in zebrafish
articles.content: Muller glia (MG) in the zebrafish retina retain a latent stem cell capacity that is absent in mammals, yet the injury responsive signals that drive this reprogramming remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), the stress-inducible, rate-limiting enzyme of heme catabolism, as a previously unrecognized regulator of this process. Following injury, hmox1a is selectively and rapidly induced among the heme oxygenase gene family, localizing to photoreceptors with expression peaking during the MG proliferation window. Pharmacological inhibition and morpholino mediated knockdown of Hmox1 dysregulate the acute inflammatory response, impair Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) proliferation, and produce lasting deficits in retinal lamination, establishing Hmox1 as a potentially non-redundant, early-acting node required for structural recovery. Exogenous delivery of carbon monoxide (CO), a bioactive Hmox1 metabolite, partially rescues each of these phenotypes, functionally implicating CO as a key downstream effector. Mechanistically, Hmox1/CO signalling stabilizes {beta}-catenin likely via transcriptional repression of the Wnt antagonist dkk1b. This stabilized {beta}-catenin is enriched at a predicted Tcf7l2 site in the promoter of vaspb, which encodes an actin binding protein and is newly identified here as an injury-induced Wnt target gene. Bioinformatic and functional analyses further implicate Nfe2l2a (Nrf2) as a candidate intermediary bridging Hmox1/CO to Wnt regulation, with putative antioxidant response elements identified within the dkk1b locus. Together, these findings outline a putative Hmox1[->]CO[->]Nrf2[->]dkk1b[->]{beta}-catenin[->]vaspb relay coupling redox biology to Wnt-dependent glial reprogramming. Notably, HO-1 is similarly induced in stressed mammalian retina, yet Wnt/{beta}-catenin activation fails to sustain regeneration, positioning the Hmox1/CO axis as a candidate target for future investigation in mammalian retina regeneration.
articles.author: Sherpa, R. D., Sen, A., Chaudhuri, A. G., Hui, S. P.

articles.title: Brain-wide representations of olfactory behavior in C. elegans
articles.content: Olfactory navigation emerges from dynamic interactions between sensory input, brain activity state and the animal's own movements. In C. elegans, a compact nervous system enables brain-wide imaging in behaving animals exposed to controlled olfactory environments, with an undulatory locomotion that reduces navigation to transitions among forward runs, reversals, and turns. Here, we used tracking microscopy to record and compare brain-wide neural activity in crawling worms navigating spatial odor gradients or isotropic environments, and in immobilized worms responding to temporal odor pulses. Across conditions, we identified strongly correlated brain-wide activity patterns spanning olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor interneurons. Comparisons between navigation in odor gradients and exploration in isotropic environments revealed a compact functional circuit linking olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor neurons. Comparisons between different odors distinguished sensory activity relationships associated with odor identity from a shared sensorimotor circuit for navigational movement. Comparisons between crawling and immobilized animals revealed profound differences in motor-state transitions and brain-wide correlation structure, further demonstrating the dependence of sensory representations and motor decision-making on behavioral context. Our findings reveal a functional organization linking olfactory sensory activity to navigational movement and show how this organization depends on behavioral state and environmental context.
articles.author: Casademunt, H., Zhang, H., Laver, J., Park, C. F., Kim, S., Fredenberg, W., Hung, W., Calarco, J., Zhen, M., Samuel, A. D. T.

articles.title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity
articles.content: Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.
articles.author: Gupta, A., Neveu, C. L., Byrne, J. H.

articles.title: Noise-referenced multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging for regional cerebrospinal fluid thermometry
articles.content: We developed a multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging approach for separate ventricular and subarachnoid cerebrospinal fluid thermometry. The approach uses measured image noise to assess agreement among temperature estimates. In 12 participants, temperature was estimated from four non-zero diffusion weightings. For each voxel, disagreement between these estimates was compared with that expected from image noise, accounting for their shared reference image. Voxels meeting this consistency criterion were retained for regional analysis. Mean diffusion-derived temperature ({+/-} SD) was 38.4 {+/-} 0.4 {degrees}C in the lateral ventricles and 36.0 {+/-} 1.1 {degrees}C in the subarachnoid space. Ventricular estimates were consistently higher than subarachnoid estimates across all participants, with a mean difference of 2.4 {+/-} 1.2 {degrees}C (95% confidence interval 1.6 -3.1 {degrees}C). This difference persisted under alternative noise models and temperature estimators. Subarachnoid estimates increased with retained voxel count; in a post hoc analysis of the six participants with the largest retained counts, ventricular estimates remained higher by 1.6 {+/-} 0.7 {degrees}C. Absolute temperature accuracy and the physiological origin of the regional difference require independent validation. This approach provides an internal consistency check for CSF thermometry and supports separate assessment of ventricular and subarachnoid temperatures.
